prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

When God appears before me he is a burning woman tied to a bush. Her nakedness, a missed spot on a busy canvas, where a male hand has been practicing female gestures. For instance, hanging herself like laundry over her own arm. Nipple-colons introduce this scene of medieval war: horses crowned with riders are leaving; horses’ tails, like a clock’s hands, whip flies of hours off their round thighs. Time is an insect that leaves its maggots to hatch on an open wound of a mammal. There’s more face on these thighs than on all of the women’s bodies. One, with an arrow aimed at her, hands on her bent knees as if she wanted to ski into death like a scared child, mocks the splendid horse tails with hair so red, all of her blood must have gone into it. So, it isn’t a bush on fire. It’s red hair she used as a shield. In the distance, a town burning. Impatiently, horses whip buzzing ashes. The end.

Here are two ways to polish the text, depending on the tone you wish to achieve. Both options retain all of your vivid imagery, metaphors, and original details while elevating the cadence, syntax, and vocabulary.

### Option 1: Refined Literary Prose (Recommended)
*This version enhances the artistic flow and elegance while maintaining the raw, surreal intensity of the original text.*

> When God appears before me, He takes the form of a burning woman bound to a bush. Her nakedness is an unpainted void upon a crowded canvas, a space where a male hand has rehearsed feminine gestures—draping herself, for instance, like laundry over her own arm. Nipple-colons introduce this scene of medieval warfare: riders crown their departing steeds, whose tails, moving like the hands of a clock, sweep the flies of hours from their rounded flanks. Time is an insect that deposits its maggots to hatch within the open wound of a mammal. Indeed, there is more countenance in these flanks than on all the women’s bodies combined. One woman—an arrow aimed at her, hands resting on her bent knees as if she wished to ski into death like a frightened child—mocks the magnificent horse tails with hair so intensely red all her blood must have drained into it. Thus, it is not a bush ablaze; it is her crimson hair, raised as a shield. In the distance, a town burns. Impatiently, the horses swat at the buzzing ashes. The end.

---

### Option 2: Poetic & Visceral Ekphrasis
*This version preserves the staccato, rhythmic punch of the original while polishing the phrasing for maximum impact.*

> Whenever God appears to me, He is a burning woman tied to a bush. Her nakedness is a missed spot on a dense canvas, a site where a male hand has practiced female postures—hanging herself, for instance, over her own arm like laundry. Nipple-colons herald this vision of medieval war: horses crowned with riders are leaving; their tails, like clock hands, whip flies of hours off their round thighs. Time is a parasite that leaves its maggots to hatch in a mammal's open wound. There is more expression on these thighs than on all the women’s bodies. One of them, an arrow trained upon her, holds her bent knees as if she might ski into death like a scared child, mocking the splendid horse tails with hair so red that all her blood must have poured into it. So, it is not a burning bush after all. It is red hair she has borne as a shield. Far off, a town burns. Impatiently, horses whip at the buzzing ashes. The end.

---

### Key Improvements Made:
* **Punctuation & Cadence:** Used em-dashes and semicolons to group complex images together, creating a smoother, more rhythmic reading experience.
* **Elevated Diction:** Replaced simpler phrasing (e.g., *"there's more face"* $\rightarrow$ *"there is more countenance"*, or *"steeds"* for *"horses"*) while preserving every surreal image (nipple-colons, skiing into death, maggots on a wound).
* **Structural Clarity:** Enhanced the transition where the image of the "burning bush" is re-evaluated as red hair acting as a shield.
outputs.L2:
My vision of the Almighty manifests not as a traditional icon, but as a flaming female figure lashed to a shrub. Her unclad body resembles a blank, unpainted void within a crowded painting, marking a spot where a male artist attempted to mimic feminine poses—demonstrated by the way she drapes limply across her own limb like wet garments on a line. 

Her breast tips act as punctuation to introduce a medieval battlefield: mounted soldiers ride away, while the steeds' tails swish across their rounded hindquarters like ticking clock hands clearing away the flying insects of passing hours. In this space, time operates like a pest, depositing its larvae to fester inside the open injury of a mammal. 

Remarkably, the legs of these animals carry far more expressive detail than the physical forms of every woman depicted. One female target of a drawn arrow crouches with her hands resting on flexed knees, resembling a terrified child sliding headlong into mortality; her hair is so intensely crimson that all her lifeblood seems to have transferred into it, mocking the splendid tails of the mounts. 

Thus, the burning bush was an illusion. In reality, she was employing her vibrant red tresses as a protective barrier. Far in the background, a settlement succumbs to flames while the restless horses swat at the humming cinders around them. The vision concludes.
outputs.L3:
In this haunting visionary tableau, the divine reveals itself not through thunderous majesty, but through a striking, paradoxical illusion. God appears to the speaker as a naked, bound woman whose vibrant, fiery red hair cascades in wild waves, contorting in the ambient light to mimic the biblical phenomenon of a burning bush. Sacredness in this space is born not of unyielding power, but of constraint, vulnerability, and artifice.

Upon closer inspection, this divine female form is fundamentally incomplete. She is framed as a blank, unfinished spot on a larger canvas—a void where a male artist has awkwardly practiced the delicate gestures of femininity. Her body bears the hesitation of a male creator attempting to draft an essence he does not fully understand, leaving the central icon of the vision caught between divine revelation and an incomplete artistic exercise.

Surrounding this figure, the backdrop opens into a gruesome medieval battlefield where time itself takes on a malignant physical form. Rather than a gentle stream or an impartial clock, time is portrayed as a parasitic insect. It hovers relentlessly over the carnage, depositing writhing maggots into the gaping, open wounds of the dying. Decay is rendered not as a passive consequence of battle, but as an active, ravenous force driving the passage of moments.

The composition reveals a disturbing set of priorities embedded within the artwork. The painter has lavished exquisite detail, movement, and vital energy onto the war horses, prioritizing their muscular beauty and expressive presence. In contrast, the vulnerable, objectified women facing imminent death are treated as mere background props—disregarded by the creator’s brush even as they confront their end. 

The vision concludes at the periphery of the frame, far from the central violence. In the distance, a nameless town burns to embers, casting a haze across the horizon. The vibrant, prioritized horses stand unbothered in the foreground, casually swatting away the buzzing, fly-like ashes of the distant fires with their tails as the scene fades into quiet ruin.
outputs.L4:
**The Flame in the Ash: Deconstructing the Divine in Medieval War**

To step before the massive, centuries-old canvas is to be immediately overwhelmed by a dense landscape of violence. The medieval battle scene is rendered with meticulous, almost clinical precision: a claustrophobic sea of gleam and gore where iron broadswords sever limbs, heavy plate armor crushes bone, and the mud drinks blood. Rendered through a male-dominated lens typical of its era, the painting treats bodies as mere raw material—objectified, brutalized, and immortalized for the sake of a grand militaristic spectacle. Yet, nestled within this chaotic tapestry of destruction, the painter has positioned a startling anomaly, a visual focal point that draws the eye like a beacon amidst the shadow and smoke.

At a distance, the viewer appears to be witnessing an act of transcendent grace. Rising from a patch of trampled earth near the fringe of the carnage is a bright, luminous mass of crimson and gold. It glows with an eerie, supernatural intensity, echoing the traditional iconography of biblical epiphanies. The immediate, instinctual interpretation—one long reinforced by patriarchal art traditions—is that of the burning bush. It reads as a divine miracle inserted into a field of death, a holy flame signaling that God is present, watching over the righteous warriors, and sanctifying the bloody endeavor. It offers a comforting narrative: that even in the horrors of war, the hand of Heaven is at work.

However, a closer, more rigorous examination shatters this pious illusion. As the viewer draws near to analyze the fine brushstrokes, the ethereal "flames" lose their abstract, divine quality and take on an intensely physical, human reality. The blazing bush is not a bush at all. It is a woman.

Stripped of divine abstraction, the image reveals a vulnerable, living subject huddled in the dirt. Surrounded by the threat of violence and the debris of fallen siege engines, she has seized control of her own body in the only way left to her. She has pulled her long, unnaturally bright red hair over her head and shoulders, fanning it out around her trembling frame. The vibrant tresses—historically objectified as symbols of dangerous temptation or passive beauty—are reappropriated into a desperate, self-fashioned armor. She uses the brilliant pigment of her own body to create a protective mantle, a visual shield meant to obscure her presence or ward off the horrors circling her.

This revelation fundamentally subverts the painting's intended narrative. By transforming what looked like a male-centric vision of divine revelation into an intimate act of female self-preservation, the image dismantles the romanticism of medieval warfare. The true "miracle" on the canvas is not a voice from a holy fire justifying the violence of men; it is the sheer, defiant ingenuity of a woman attempting to survive it. 

Ultimately, the text of the painting turns in on itself. It demonstrates how male-dominated histories have historically reframed female suffering and survival as mere background decoration or divine symbolism. By recognizing the red hair for what it is—a shield rather than a sacred flame—the observer uncovers a quiet, disturbing truth: that amidst the catastrophic noise of male conquest, the most profound revelation is not the presence of a god, but the fierce, resilient agency of a woman claiming her right to endure.
outputs.L5:
People often ask **when** the divine chooses to reveal itself. They look toward the distant stars, search through ancient texts, or wait for the thunderous voice of **God** to echo from the sky. But grace rarely arrives with a grand fanfare. More often than not, it steps quietly into a room, disguised in the ordinary moments we so easily overlook.

For me, revelation did not come on a lonely mountain peak or in a solemn cathedral. It arrived on a rainy Tuesday, simply by looking into the eyes of **her**.

There was no burning bush or choir of angels—just the quiet rhythm of **her** voice, the steady warmth of **her** hand resting in mine, and a sudden, undeniable clarity. In **her** capacity for forgiveness, I finally understood the true nature of mercy. In **her** laughter, I found a lightness that felt older and deeper than the world itself. It was as if the universe had condensed all its boundless love into a single, breathing presence.

**When** you see the sacred reflected so clearly in another human being, your entire perspective shifts. You begin to realize that **God** is not merely a distant architect watching from above, but an active, living current woven through our everyday lives. **God** exists in the patience she offers to a world in a hurry, the beauty she finds in broken things, and the quiet sanctuary she creates just by being who she is.

So, **when** I am asked where I find my faith, I no longer point toward the clouds. I think of the quiet grace of **her**, and I know that the divine has been right beside me all along.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short prose poem opening with a subversion of Moses and the burning bush, blending surreal art criticism, medieval war imagery, and feminist themes.
counterfactuals.output: She did not take off her sandals before the burning bush; she merely adjusted her glass and declared the composition derivative. It was not the Father who spoke from the thistled blaze, but a chorus of forgotten conscripts, their larynxes forged from boiled leather and medieval iron. "The palette relies far too heavily on patriarchal crimson," she noted, tracing the contours of the unconsumed leaves with a palette knife. The shrub was a surrealist assemblage—a miniature siege engine of thorn and tendon, dripping with an impasto of uncredited female labor. There were no tablets of law waiting in the smoke, only the warped frame of a holy war that had long stretched women's hides over its canvas. The voice did not command her to bow; it demanded a total re-evaluation of the gallery. And so, keeping her shoes firmly on, she stepped through the burning medium, leaving the shepherd alone in the desert with nothing to worship but the cracked varnish of his own authority.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you generate an experimental prose poem that critiques male artistic depictions of female trauma in historical war paintings? Make the language uncanny, surreal, and vividly descriptive, ending abruptly with "The end."
counterfactuals.output: The master adjusts his velvet collar and dips a single boar bristle into the liquid dusk of her ruined socket. Observe the geometry of the sack: her linen tunic torn at precisely thirty degrees, a calculated slip of weave exposing just enough pearl-toned ribs to balance the diagonal thrust of the conqueror’s spear. He has varnished her panic with boiled walnut oil so her terror reflects the gallery chandeliers, bright, smooth, and endlessly collectible. Outside the frame, the city is actual meat and ash, but here, upon the stretched linen, her disembowelment is merely a triumph of *sfumato*. Her screams do not sound; they solidify into tiny, polished pebbles of zinc white, which the painter sweeps into a velvet pouch to trade for port. Look how lovingly he glazes the purple rim of the bayonet wound, softening the gangrene into a romantic, bruised mauve that pairs well with mahogany sideboards. Her fingers, frozen in an eternal, graceful plea toward a sky he painted out, have been lengthened by three inches to better balance the composition against the dark mass of horse rumps. She cannot fall; the dried resin has locked her spine into an exquisite, arching backbend. Gentlemen in cravats gather to debate the light technique of her violation, stroking their chins over the soft, translucent blue of her dying veins. Her mouth remains a dry knot of crimson lake, choked on three centuries of silent museum dust. The end.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a piece of dark ekphrastic prose describing a strange, disturbing medieval battle painting. Focus on visceral metaphors regarding time, horses, red hair, and the female body.
counterfactuals.output:
The oil has long since oxidized into the shade of bruised lard, but the violence beneath the varnish remains hideously wet. 

The painter—some anonymous madman of the fourteenth century—did not render a battle; he rendered the digestion of a world. The canvas is choked with the geometry of slaughter, where time does not flow, but congeals like cooling tallow. It hangs over the skirmish like a swollen, yellowed sun: a clock with no hands, only a blind, milky eye that freezes the iron and the marrow at the precise instant of rupture. In this painted hell, a second is an eternity stretching until the fabric snaps; the centuries have merely rotted the edges of a single, perpetual scream.

At the center, the horses are not beasts of burden, but shrieking engines of muscle and terror. Their bellies, split open by billhooks, spill coils of wet intestine that tangle with the stirrups like the rusted gears of a broken clock. Their eyes are glass globes reflecting a sky the color of dried bile. They do not trample the earth; they emerge from it, their black hooves crushing the skulls of foot-soldier infants, their necks twisting at unnatural, dislocating angles. One stallion’s jaw is unhinged entirely, vomiting not foam, but a black, tarry liquid that pools around the feet of the dying.

Spilling through the black mud like an open artery is a torrent of red hair. It does not belong to the sun, nor to any natural dye, but to a violent, copper flame that writhes across the lower third of the frame. It belongs to a woman fallen beneath the writhing mass of horseflesh and iron. Her hair is an infectious parasite, braiding itself around rusted spaulders, pulling down knights by their throats, choking the wooden spokes of war-carts. It is wet, heavy, and bright as a freshly sheared nerve.

Her body is the altar upon which the canvas performs its darkest sacrilege. Stripped of mail, her skin is the stark, sickening white of peeled birch, contrasting grotesquely against the mud and iron. The painter has subverted the holy pity of the *Pieta*; her torso is stretched, her ribs parted like the arches of a ruined cathedral to expose a hollow chest where no heart beats. Her hipbones curve upward like the pincer-jaws of a burrowing insect, framing a belly that is pale, soft, and impossibly smooth amidst the jagged steel. 

She is at once the victim and the sovereign of the carnage. From her open mouth, a single thread of that coarse red hair trails back into the sky, tethering her torn, luminous body to the dead sun above. Around her, time, war, and beast are locked in an agonizing stillness: a horse forever falling, a blade forever hovering above a pale throat, and her copper hair forever drinking the black grease of the earth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: "When God appears before me he is..." Write a brief surreal narrative starting with this line.
counterfactuals.output:
When God appears before me he is a migratory flock of porcelain teacups flying across my living room ceiling. 

They hum in a quiet C-sharp, their saucers clinking together like soft, bone-china applause. I offer him a spoonful of sugar, but he politely declines by reassembling himself into a tall gentleman composed entirely of late-afternoon sunlight and old television static. 

"You left the porch light on," he says. His voice smells faintly of burnt toast and wet asphalt.

"I was waiting for you," I reply, standing on a chair made of melted wax so I can reach his collar. 

He reaches into his trench coat pocket—which is actually a spiral staircase descending into an upside-down ocean—and pulls out a silver pocket watch. When he clicks it open, there are no gears inside, only a tiny, perfectly preserved loop of my seventh birthday party. A miniature version of me blows out candles made of trapped lightning.

"Is it time?" I ask. 

God smiles, folding his hands until they turn into a pair of origami cranes. "Not yet. The clocks are still sleeping."

He places one of the paper birds gently in my palm. It warm-breathes against my thumb, and with a soft *snap*, the carpet beneath us dissolves into a knee-deep lake of lukewarm lavender milk. Before I can sink, God unties his shoes, steps directly into the ceiling, and disappears into a rainstorm that falls upward, splashing quietly against the stars.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe a terrifying visual vision that combines divine revelation, grotesque art analysis, and a burning medieval town in a modern poetic voice.
counterfactuals.output:
The sky is a heavy impasto of charcoal and burnt sienna, 
slathered thick over a XV-century horizon. 
The village is breaking down into its base elements: 
oak-frame, pig fat, dry thatch, and panic. 
Notice the brushwork of the fire—
erratic, hungry strokes of toxic lead-tin yellow 
licking the bell tower until the iron melts like tallow.

And then, the tear in the canvas.

It does not open like a curtain; it splits like dry skin.
The revelation is an asymmetric geometry,
a hyper-saturated, un-rendered light that violates the color wheel.
It is an angel, if you insist on archaic taxonomy,
but look at the formal composition:
a terrifying assemblage of interlocking wheels, 
rimmed with wet, blinking irises, floating in a sea of boiling gold leaf.
There is no human grace here, no Renaissance symmetry—
only a brutal, suffocating holiness.
It shouts *BE NOT AFRAID* in a pitch that shatters the ribcages 
of the weavers screaming on the cobblestones below.

Consider the grotesque efficiency of the foreground:
a mother, mid-scream, her face foreshortened with brutal accuracy,
her mouth a dark, hollow ellipse framed by blistering skin.
The texture of the horror is exquisitely rendered—
the way the heat causes the human fat to sizzle against wet stone,
the chiaroscuro of a burning pig running through a dark alleyway,
casting long, distorted shadows that mirror the nightmare above.

The divine entity does not come to save; 
it comes to be witnessed.
It casts a high-definition, clinical glare over the catastrophe,
illuminating every rupture, every spewed intestine, every charred prayer,
with the cold, unblinking clarity of a gallery spotlight.

The truth revealed is not mercy. 
The truth is that the fire, the screaming town, 
the boiling eye-rimmed wheels, and the artist 
are all made of the exact same light—
and the frame is closing in.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
